text:
**Express Lane**

The first thing Marnie Hale knew about Teddy Pruitt was that he bought the wrong things. He came through her line at Harvey's on a Tuesday in March with a single lemon, a box of cat treats, and a birthday candle shaped like the number seven, and he set them on the belt in a row, as if presenting evidence.

"Ten items or fewer," she said, because it was the sort of thing she said. There were three items.

"I counted," Teddy said. "I'm well under."

She had been a cashier for eleven years, long enough to sort people by what they put on the belt. The Sunday-circular people, with coupons banded like small bouquets. A man with a lemon, cat treats, and a seven-shaped candle belonged to no category she had, and she looked at him longer than she meant to. He was perhaps thirty-four, soft in the middle, with the faintly startled look of a man who has been told he is handsome only by relatives. His shirt was ironed. Nobody she knew ironed.

"Is it for a person or a cat?" she asked. "The candle."

"A person. She's seven. My cousin's." He considered. "The lemon's for me."

He came back Thursday and bought a pear. By the third week he was waiting in her line even when others were shorter, and Keisha at the next register began humming the wedding march whenever he appeared. Marnie told her to hush. She was thirty-seven and had been married once, briefly, to a man who sold above-ground pools and then disappeared into Tennessee, and she had no expectation that a person who ironed his shirts would want her. Yet in the second week of May, on a day so humid the automatic doors seemed to exhale at them, Teddy asked whether she would like to drive to the courthouse in Hillsboro with him, and she said yes before she understood it was not a figure of speech.

---

He told her about his mother on the drive, in the careful tone of a man describing weather he couldn't control. "She's a lot. People call her Miss Emily. Even people who've known her thirty years. Even the bank."

"Is that a Southern thing?"

"It's a her thing."

Emily Pruitt had started with one hardware store in 1983, a cinder-block building on Route 70 that her husband had inherited and was prepared to let die. He died instead, of a heart that had apparently been planning it, and Emily, thirty-one, took the store and the debt and a bookkeeping course and made Pruitt Home & Garden, which now had eleven locations across two states and a regional jingle. *Pruitt's has it, Pruitt's has it, if you can dream it, Pruitt's has it.*

"Does she know we're doing this?"

"I'll tell her after. She's better with accomplished facts."

They were married by a clerk with a cold, in a room that smelled of carpet cleaner, with Keisha as a witness. Afterward they ate pancakes, and Marnie, looking at the plain band Teddy had bought the previous Saturday, which fit too loosely, thought she had never done a thing so unlike her, and did not feel unlike herself at all. That was the frightening part.

---

Miss Emily received them the following Sunday at the house on Laurel Ridge. Brick, white columns that weren't quite structural, a lawn so even it looked varnished. Miss Emily met them in the front hall, a small woman, much smaller than her reputation, with close-cut silver hair and the posture of someone who has spent decades making sure no one is standing behind her.

"So this is the accomplished fact," she said.

"Mama," Teddy said.

"I'm teasing, Theodore. Come here." She took Marnie's hand in both of hers, and Marnie was aware of it: chipped polish, chapped knuckle from the cold case at work, the ring. Miss Emily looked at the ring a long moment. "Well. We'll fix that. It's loose, honey. You'll lose it down a drain."

It was the first of many things Miss Emily noticed, and it took Marnie weeks to understand the noticing was not hostile. It was inventory. Miss Emily surveyed a person the way she surveyed a shelf: what was there, what was missing, what had been placed at eye level that should have been placed lower. At lunch, served by a woman named Pearline whom no one introduced, she asked where Marnie's people were from, and Marnie said Dunn, her mother was in a facility in Smithfield now, her father had left when she was nine.

"And you ran a register how long?"

"Eleven years."

"I hired a girl once who'd run a register. Best employee I ever had. She could tell you the total before the machine did." She buttered a roll. "You can do that?"

"Most of the time. If it's under a hundred."

"Hm," said Miss Emily, the most approving sound Marnie would hear from her for a year.

---

They moved into the guest house behind the main one, a decision made, like most decisions, in advance. It had a stove that had never been lit and a view of Miss Emily's kitchen window, which Marnie learned to avoid looking at after dark. Teddy worked for the company in a capacity she found hard to pin down: an office at the Raleigh headquarters and something called vendor relationships, which seemed to involve lunch. He was kind, and funny in a way that arrived late, after a silence, so she often laughed a beat behind him and he looked pleased anyway. He was also a man who had never once been told no by anything that mattered, and who therefore treated the world as a soft, accommodating thing, like a sofa.

She had expected to feel poor among these people. She hadn't expected to feel *loud*. On Laurel Ridge the quiet had a texture, like felt. Miss Emily's friends, women with good teeth and boiled-looking pearls, spoke in low voices about the symphony and someone's hip, and when Marnie spoke she heard her voice go out into that quiet like a dropped tray.

"You say *ain't*," Miss Emily observed one evening, not unkindly, as they arranged forks for a dinner of twelve.

"Do I?"

"Once or twice. It's not a crime. But you'll want to know it's there. My mother said it until the day she died, and it kept her from a good many things."

Marnie held a fork and thought of several answers. She thought of her own mother, who said *ain't* and *y'all* and *I swan*, and who had for twenty years cleaned the offices of a tire distributor and raised a daughter on what she found in the wastebaskets: pens, mostly, and once a perfectly good umbrella. "All right," she said instead. "Thank you for telling me."

Miss Emily looked at her sharply. Marnie understood she had passed a test, though not one she wanted to pass.

---

That summer Miss Emily began to take her along: the florist, the lawyer's office, and then, in July, a store. The oldest, the cinder-block building on Route 70, which Miss Emily refused to renovate and which smelled the way hardware stores do, of oil and cut keys and rubber. A man named Dwight, who had worked there since 1986, came out from behind the counter and kissed Miss Emily on the cheek, and she let him.

"Now watch," Miss Emily said, and stood Marnie at the register and said nothing more. For forty minutes Marnie watched people buy things. A man bought a single hinge and stood holding it, not leaving. A woman bought four bags of potting soil and a trowel, her eyes red.

"What did you see?" Miss Emily asked in the car.

"The man with the hinge didn't need a hinge."

"What did he need?"

"Somebody to ask him what was broken."

Miss Emily was silent for the length of a red light. "Dwight asked him. He always asks. I've been trying for twenty years to put that in a training manual. You can't. It turns out you can't."

It was the nearest thing to a compliment Marnie had had in a long time, and she held it all afternoon like something warm in her pocket. Then that night at the long table Miss Emily said to a friend, in front of her, "Marnie's so good with the public. It's the register. Those girls have a kind of instinct." And Marnie, passing the rolls, felt the warm thing go cold, because she had been shown a door and told, in the same breath, which side of it she lived on.

---

In September Teddy's cousin turned eight, and the family gathered at the lake. Marnie had looked forward to it for a week, for the candle she had bought herself and hidden in a drawer, an eight in blue wax. But there was a caterer, and a tent, and a cake made by a man in Durham who did only cakes, and no one wanted the candle. She put it in her purse.

She stood at the edge of the dock with a glass of something that tasted of cucumber and watched Teddy teach the little girl to skip stones. He was patient. He crouched and showed her the flat of his hand, the flick of the wrist. She loved him, she thought, with surprise, as one loves a house one has lived in for months before noticing the light in the kitchen.

"He was a lonely boy," said Miss Emily, who had come up beside her without a sound. "I worked all the time. I put him in front of a television and went to open another store. I'm not sorry. But I knew what it cost." She was looking at the water. "I wanted him to marry someone from the club. I had a girl in mind. And then he came home with a woman who looked at my ring finger before she looked at my face, and I thought, well. She counts."

"I didn't mean—"

"Don't apologize. It was the right order." Miss Emily's mouth moved slightly. "You'll wear the good ring Saturday. I've had it sized."

---

The good ring was Emily's mother-in-law's, a cushion-cut diamond in old platinum, and when it was on her finger Marnie kept turning it toward her palm, as she had once turned the shiny side of a coupon inward. She wore it to Harvey's, which she visited in October out of a feeling she couldn't name.

Keisha was on register four, and Marnie stood in her long line behind a woman with a cart full of juice boxes, holding a single lemon. She watched Keisha's hands, the quick tilt of the wrist, the *Hey, baby, how you doing today* said without looking up, and felt the beeping and fluorescent hum of that life rise around her again. She wasn't homesick. It was stranger. She felt like a visitor to a place that had gone on, quite rudely, without her.

"Look at you," Keisha said at the front. She took Marnie's hand, turned it over, and whistled low. "Girl. That's a *rock*."

"It's Miss Emily's mother-in-law's."

"It's on your hand." Keisha scanned the lemon. "Forty-nine cents. You want to tell me it's all right? Over there?"

Marnie thought of the quiet and the forks, of Pearline, whom nobody introduced, of the hinge man, and how a person can be handed everything and still stand at a counter holding one small thing, not leaving.

"It's all right. It's not like I thought."

"Is she mean to you?"

"No." And this was the part she couldn't say to Keisha, who had a whole vocabulary for meanness. "She's just paying attention."

Keisha handed over the lemon with a little flourish. "That's worse," she said. "Ain't it?"

"Yes," Marnie said, and heard the word leave her mouth, and let it stand.

---

In November Miss Emily asked her to come to headquarters. The sky was low and the color of dishwater, and Marnie drove herself, a small defiance she kept to herself. Miss Emily's office, on the fourth floor of the glass building, had a window onto the parking lot, which surprised her. Miss Emily shrugged. "I like to see who's coming in."

On the desk was a folder. "I'm not going to give you a title. I'm saying that now, so you don't wait for one. I'm going to give you a Tuesday and a Thursday. You'll go to the stores. The old ones, the failing ones, there are three. You'll stand at the register and tell me what you see."

"Why me?"

"Because everybody else I send, the store sees them coming. They put out the good display. You look like a customer. You look like someone who's tired. They won't change a thing for you."

It was both an honor and an insult, and Miss Emily knew it, and was waiting to see which Marnie would choose. For a moment she was angry in a clear, cold way she hadn't been since the pool salesman left. Then she thought of her mother scrubbing the tire distributor's floors, and of the particular dignity of being looked at by someone who finds you useful. It was not love. But she had been alive long enough to know that most of what holds people together is not love but use, mutual and unspoken, like a pair of hands on opposite ends of a heavy table.

"Tuesdays and Thursdays," she said. "And I'll want to be paid."

Miss Emily's face opened, briefly, into a real smile, and closed again. "Of course you'll be paid. What do you take me for?"

---

That night she told Teddy, who lay on the guest house sofa with the cat on his chest, a cat that had materialized in October and been named Pruitt over her objections. He was quiet for his customary beat, and then said, "She's never asked me to do anything like that."

"She asked you to run vendor relationships."

"That's a thing she made up so I'd have a thing." He said it without bitterness, scratching the cat's jaw. "I always knew."

She sat on the arm of the sofa. Across the dark lawn, Miss Emily was a small figure behind her kitchen glass, wiping a counter Pearline had already wiped. Marnie had stopped avoiding that window sometime in October without noticing.

"Do you mind?"

"No." He looked up with that startled, soft face. "I think it's the nicest thing she's ever done. She just did it for you instead of me. You'll be better at it."

"I will," Marnie said, and surprised herself, and he laughed, a beat late, and she laughed with him, on time.

She took the blue candle out of her purse and set it on the sill, a little crooked, among the dust and dead flies. Across the lawn, Miss Emily switched off her light. Marnie stood a moment longer in the dark, turning the heavy ring toward her palm and then, deliberately, away.
